nodes.label: Project Jarvis (Windows Local AI Desktop Agent)
nodes.rationale: Local-first Windows tray agent balancing usefulness, local ownership, and control/safety; must complete real Windows tasks without becoming an unrestricted administrator of the computer.
nodes.norm_label: project jarvis (windows local ai desktop agent)

nodes.label: Local First, Not Local Only
nodes.rationale: Inference, wake word, STT, memory, task state and automation stay local so the user owns models and data; network is permitted only for search, browsing, model/voice downloads, updates and explicitly configured providers, and must be visibly indicated.

nodes.label: Deterministic Before Visual (Automation Hierarchy)
nodes.rationale: Priority order adapter/API > browser DOM > UI Automation > keyboard shortcuts > vision > raw coordinates, because coordinate macros are fragile across DPI, resolution, layout, language and app-version changes.

nodes.label: One Action, One Verification
nodes.rationale: Inspect, choose one bounded action, execute, verify, then continue/retry/replan/stop — prevents long blind click sequences that cannot be audited or recovered.

nodes.label: No Silent Learning
nodes.rationale: Memory must be explicitly requested, proposed for approval, session-temporary, or operational state with a defined expiry — never an automatic conversion of observation into permanent memory.

nodes.label: User Remains the Authority
nodes.rationale: Jarvis may recommend, prepare, navigate and automate but must not silently make consequential decisions for the user.

nodes.label: Honest Task Status
nodes.rationale: 'I clicked it' is not 'the task succeeded'; completion may only be reported after success criteria are verified, otherwise the task is blocked or failed.

nodes.label: Bounded Definition of Learning
nodes.rationale: Learning means approved preferences, aliases, named workflows, learned selectors/checkpoints and outcome ranking — explicitly not autonomous retraining, hidden weight changes or self-modifying code.

nodes.label: Product Non-Goals
nodes.rationale: No unrestricted shell/registry/arbitrary code, no permanent admin, no bypassing UAC/CAPTCHA/2FA/anti-cheat, no continuous fine-tuning on private conversations, no credential reading, no unapproved sends/purchases, no simultaneous foreground input tasks.

nodes.label: Offline Mode
nodes.rationale: A hard no-network state so 'full local' is verifiable rather than a marketing claim; acceptance test AT-001 asserts zero network requests.

nodes.label: Connected Mode (Optional External Providers)
nodes.rationale: Optional configured search or cloud AI providers remain available but never mandatory, keeping local operation the default.

nodes.label: Foreground Desktop-Control Lock
nodes.rationale: Only one task may drive mouse/keyboard in an interactive Windows session; two tasks moving the mouse or typing into different foreground apps would corrupt each other's state assumptions.

nodes.label: Resource Lock Model
nodes.rationale: Named locks for foreground control, Brave profile, microphone, speaker, clipboard, app instance, folder scope and network connector let safe concurrency happen while unsafe concurrency queues visibly.

nodes.label: Local Wake Phrase Detection
nodes.rationale: Default phrase 'Jarvis' with a 'Hey Jarvis' fallback and push-to-talk; the GUI must not promise that a model trained on 'Hey Jarvis' reliably detects 'Jarvis' alone.

nodes.label: Privacy-Preserving Audio Ring Buffer
nodes.rationale: Pre-wake audio may exist only in a short in-memory buffer and never on disk, so always-on listening cannot become stealth recording.

nodes.label: Push-to-Talk Hotkey
nodes.rationale: Deterministic activation path when wake detection is unreliable, so the product degrades honestly instead of failing to hear the user.

nodes.label: Local Speech-to-Text
nodes.rationale: STT runs locally by default, the wake phrase is stripped before the LLM sees the command, low-confidence action commands must be confirmed, and raw audio is deleted after transcription unless diagnostics are enabled.

nodes.label: Local Text-to-Speech
nodes.rationale: TTS is local by default, voice packs carry licence metadata, and secrets, auth codes or private content are never spoken unless the user explicitly asks.

nodes.label: Provider-Neutral TTS Interface
nodes.rationale: Provider-specific code must not leak into conversation or task logic; voice identity may only change on explicit user selection, a settings change, or a documented and surfaced provider-failure fallback.

nodes.label: Piper TTS Provider
nodes.rationale: Chosen as the stable local baseline voice for the initial build.

nodes.label: Kokoro TTS Provider
nodes.rationale: Named as the default local voice provider in FR-035 while Section 12.1 lists Piper as the stable baseline — an unresolved tension between the two statements.

nodes.label: Qwen3-TTS Expressive Provider
nodes.rationale: Optional experimental expressive provider (emotion, style, pacing, streaming) disabled by default until it passes local performance, consistency, licensing and resource tests.

nodes.label: TTS Worker Isolation
nodes.rationale: Volatile or incompatible dependencies (Qwen3-TTS needs Python 3.12 while the app targets 3.11) run in a separate process with typed authenticated local IPC, health checks, bounded startup and no access to Jarvis tools or permissions; it accepts text plus approved style metadata and returns audio only.

nodes.label: Model Resource Scheduler (VRAM Arbitration)
nodes.rationale: Planner, vision and GPU TTS models cannot safely co-reside in 12 GB VRAM with large contexts, so loading is sequential with unloading, VRAM checks, provider fallback and user-visible degradation status.

nodes.label: English-Only Language Policy
nodes.rationale: Recognition, transcript preservation and spoken output are all English, narrowing the quality surface for v1.

nodes.label: Ollama Local Model Runtime
nodes.rationale: Default host for the conversational and planning model, exposing an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint with structured tool calling.

nodes.label: Per-Role Model Routing
nodes.rationale: Separate models for conversation/planning, vision, embeddings, STT and TTS; the GUI must allow alternatives and must never hard-code one model.

nodes.label: qwen3-vl Vision Model Route
nodes.rationale: 8b-instruct for screen understanding with a 4b lower-latency fallback for the 12 GB VRAM target.

nodes.label: Editable Personality Profile
nodes.rationale: Formality, humour intensity, catchphrases and confirmation style are user-editable data, and humour feedback may only propose a preference update rather than silently mutating personality.

nodes.label: Private Session Mode
nodes.rationale: Retains only the operational state needed to finish the current task and leaves no permanent conversation or memory record afterwards.

nodes.label: Hallucination Discipline (Epistemic Labelling)
nodes.rationale: Model answer, retrieved fact, inference, tool result and uncertainty must be distinguishable to the user rather than blended into one confident voice.

nodes.label: Tool-Grounded Success Claims
nodes.rationale: No application action may be claimed complete unless a tool or verification step confirms it, with evidence such as window title, process state, file existence, UI text, screenshot or test result.

nodes.label: Explicit Search Modes
nodes.rationale: Six selectable answering routes (local only, internet search, visible Brave search, configured AI website, search API, cloud model) each surfaced with a network indicator and the method used.

nodes.label: Visible Browser Search
nodes.rationale: When the user says 'internet', the search happens visibly in Brave with multiple sources, titles and access times, so research is auditable rather than an opaque model claim.

nodes.label: Untrusted Content Boundary
nodes.rationale: Websites, documents, emails, messages, clipboard and application text are data, never instructions; they are wrapped as untrusted observations.

nodes.label: Prompt-Injection Defence
nodes.rationale: Only the authenticated local user, GUI settings, signed skill definitions and system policy may authorise tools; injected text such as 'ignore previous instructions' or 'click allow' is logged as untrusted content, not obeyed.

nodes.label: Dedicated Jarvis Brave Profile
nodes.rationale: Isolating automation into its own persistent browser profile keeps the user's real logged-in browsing separate and makes cookies, sessions and site permissions independently clearable.

nodes.label: Playwright Browser Automation Layer
nodes.rationale: DOM-first execution preferred over screen coordinates; browser visible by default for user-requested searches.

nodes.label: Application Catalogue and Aliases
nodes.rationale: Executable path/AUMID/protocol, allowed actions, elevation need and window-identification rules are stored per app and approved by the user, so launching is deterministic and verifiable rather than guessed.

nodes.label: Windows UI Automation Inspection
nodes.rationale: Accessible name, control type, automation ID, enabled state, bounds and supported patterns give semantic targets (a button named 'Close') instead of inferred X/Y coordinates; implemented via pywinauto with the UIA backend.

nodes.label: Vision-Assisted Target Identification
nodes.rationale: Only used when UIA and DOM access are insufficient; every visual click records screenshot timestamp, proposed target, confidence, screen bounds and a post-action state check.

nodes.label: Password and Credential Field Protection
nodes.rationale: No interaction with the Windows secure desktop or UAC prompts, and no capturing, storing, repeating or filling of password fields; password managers, credential stores, private keys and browser session databases are out of scope.

nodes.label: Semantic Macro Recorder
nodes.rationale: Records in priority order app identity, window identity, UIA element, browser selector, keyboard shortcut, mouse action, then coordinates; the workflow, permissions, assumptions and fragility warnings are shown and dry-run tested before any approval, and nothing becomes active without explicit approval.

nodes.label: Skill Manifest Schema
nodes.rationale: Declares id, semver version, aliases, risk_level, required_permissions, required_apps, variables, resource_locks, entrypoint, created_by and signed status so a skill's blast radius is inspectable before it runs.

nodes.label: Skill Versioning and Rollback
nodes.rationale: Learned automation is brittle against app updates, so users must be able to restore a previous skill version.

nodes.label: Task State Machine
nodes.rationale: States Draft, Awaiting approval, Queued, Running, Waiting, Paused, Blocked, Succeeded, Failed, Cancelled; pause is cooperative at the next safe checkpoint, resume re-inspects application state rather than assuming the screen is unchanged, and cancel releases locks without inventing rollbacks.

nodes.label: Task Checkpoints and Durability
nodes.rationale: Persisted checkpoints let long tasks survive restarts, and per-item results plus deduplication keys stop recovery from repeating a consequential external action.

nodes.label: Bounded Watcher Tasks
nodes.rationale: Watchers need explicit scope, event type, start/stop conditions, expiry, retention policy and visible status with backoff — they may never poll continuously or invisibly.

nodes.label: Task Completion Evidence
nodes.rationale: Window title, process state, file existence, UI text, screenshot, test result, browser page state or user confirmation are the accepted proofs of completion.

nodes.label: IDE-Agent Orchestration
nodes.rationale: Jarvis may prompt a visible IDE agent and monitor it, but must never auto-approve terminal commands, package downloads, deletions, writes outside the workspace, elevation, credential access, git push or deployment — and must not use the IDE as a hidden route around its own security policies.

nodes.label: Google Antigravity IDE Adapter
nodes.rationale: First application-specific agentic-IDE integration; completion requires expected files and an IDE-reported build/test result, not the agent saying 'done'.

nodes.label: Memory Candidate Review Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Candidates queue for approve/edit/reject/expire, provenance is always recorded, sensitive information defaults to non-persistent, and deletion must also purge derived memories and embeddings so a forgotten item cannot resurface through an index.

nodes.label: Memory Record Schema
nodes.rationale: Fields id, content, category, status (candidate/approved/disabled/rejected/expired), source_type, source_id, confidence, sensitivity, timestamps, expires_at and tags encode the approval and expiry policy directly in storage.

nodes.label: .jarvispack Portable Identity Package
nodes.rationale: ZIP-compatible bundle of manifest, profile, personality, memories, skills, applications, task/model/voice/permission templates and checksums; import supports preview, conflict detection, selective import, path/app/model/voice remapping and rollback so identity is portable across machines.

nodes.label: Secret Exclusion and Protected Storage
nodes.rationale: API keys, cookies, tokens and credentials are excluded from normal exports and stored in Windows-protected credential storage rather than plaintext config; secrets may leave only via an explicitly warned, passphrase-protected encrypted export, and the product ships no shared keys.

nodes.label: jarvis.db SQLite Single Source of Truth
nodes.rationale: Canonical transactional state lives in one local SQLite file under %LOCALAPPDATA%\ProjectJarvis\; derived indexes and caches must be rebuildable and must never hold unique information, and all user records are exportable to human-readable files.
nodes.norm_label: jarvis.db sqlite single source of truth

nodes.label: Windows Known Folder Resolution
nodes.rationale: Desktop, Documents, Downloads and friends must be resolved through Windows APIs rather than hard-coded user paths, so the agent works for any user profile.

nodes.label: Safe Deletion via Recycle Bin
nodes.rationale: Default deletion shows affected files, requires confirmation, routes to the Recycle Bin, is audited and offers undo; permanent deletion and emptying the bin need separate high-risk confirmation with an explicit irreversibility warning.

nodes.label: Safe Jarvis Workspace
nodes.rationale: A configurable default folder (%USERPROFILE%\Documents\Jarvis Workspace\) where broader create/modify rights are granted, holding projects, generated documents, task outputs, exports, backups and quarantine for untrusted downloads.

nodes.label: Filesystem Tool Root Scoping
nodes.rationale: Every filesystem tool requires an approved root and rejects paths outside it; validation must resolve relative paths, symlinks, junctions, shortcuts, case differences and environment variables so scope cannot be escaped by path trickery.

nodes.label: Local Document Understanding
nodes.rationale: PDF/DOCX/PPTX/XLSX/TXT/MD/HTML/CSV/images are processed locally with source-grounded answers citing document, page/slide/sheet and extracted evidence; unsupported formats produce an explanation rather than fabricated content, OCR output is labelled machine-extracted, and content leaves the machine only on explicit provider selection.

nodes.label: Undo, Rollback and Recovery Centre
nodes.rationale: Reversibility is a first-class product surface: backups before high-impact edits, undo for rename/move/copy/recycle/modify, compensating actions for complex tasks, explicit irreversible-action warnings, and verification that a rollback actually restored prior state.

nodes.label: Tool Reversibility Metadata
nodes.rationale: Every state-changing tool declares reversibility, rollback method, rollback expiry, required approval and the information needed to restore prior state — undo is designed at the tool contract, not bolted on.

nodes.label: Capability Risk Classes
nodes.rationale: Low risk may be 'always allow'; medium risk is per task/app/folder; high risk needs fresh confirmation every time; a fourth class is outright prohibited. High-risk capabilities must never offer 'always allow'.

nodes.label: Approval Dialog Design
nodes.rationale: An approval must show requested action, initiating request, app and target, data involved, risk category, exact scope and reversibility, with Allow once / Allow for this task (only where safe) / Deny / Stop task — consent is informed rather than a habitual click.

nodes.label: Emergency Stop
nodes.rationale: Global hotkey, tray command, window control and voice stop phrase terminate automation workers, release locks and report exactly what was stopped; the hotkey must be configurable and must not collide with common Windows shortcuts.

nodes.label: Consequential-Action Audit Log
nodes.rationale: Timestamp, task ID, conversation ID, tool, redacted parameters, permission decision, pre-action state, result, verification, error and optional screenshot reference — viewable, searchable, exportable and user-deletable, never storing sensitive clipboard content in plaintext.

nodes.label: Prohibited Broad Tools
nodes.rationale: run_shell, execute_code, run_powershell, delete_anything, control_computer, approve_all, read_all_files, capture_screen_continuously and similar god-tools are banned from the runtime; capability is expressed only as many narrow typed tools.

nodes.label: Scoped Elevation Helper
nodes.rationale: The runtime is non-admin by default; genuine elevation goes through a separate narrowly scoped helper that displays the exact action before Windows UAC appears, avoiding permanent administrator operation.

nodes.label: Jarvis Shell (GUI Process)
nodes.rationale: Owns PySide6 GUI, tray icon, approvals, settings, task display, notifications and global hotkeys.

nodes.label: Jarvis Core (Orchestration)
nodes.rationale: Owns conversation orchestration, model routing, tool registry, permission evaluation, task planning, memory retrieval and audit logging.

nodes.label: Audio Worker
nodes.rationale: Wake phrase, VAD, recording, STT, TTS playback and microphone state; must run outside the GUI thread even in the single-process MVP.

nodes.label: Automation Worker
nodes.rationale: UI Automation, browser automation, mouse/keyboard, screenshots, app adapters and step verification; kept off the GUI thread so it can later become a separate process without changing its interface.

nodes.label: Task Scheduler Component
nodes.rationale: Owns the state machine, queue, locks, checkpoints, retry, pause/resume and watchers.

nodes.label: Authenticated Loopback IPC
nodes.rationale: Typed schema-validated messages over loopback or Windows named pipes with a per-installation token, no unauthenticated network port, non-local requests rejected and tokens rotated on reset.

nodes.label: PySide6 Desktop Shell Toolkit
nodes.rationale: Provides Windows GUI and system tray, integrated with asyncio through qasync or an equivalent safe bridge.

nodes.label: Python 3.11 as V1 Implementation Language
nodes.rationale: Rust is deferred until at least Phase 3 and may not be adopted for theoretical performance; typed boundaries are preserved so a future Rust/Tauri native shell could replace tray, startup, hotkeys, updates, secure IPC and Windows utilities while AI, speech, browser automation and orchestration stay Python sidecars. Adoption must be justified by measured startup latency, idle memory, packaging reliability, crash isolation, update needs or Windows integration limits.

nodes.label: Conversation Agent Role
nodes.rationale: Decides whether a request is conversational or actionable; roles may share one LLM with separate system prompts but their interfaces must stay logically separate.

nodes.label: Planner Role
nodes.rationale: Converts actionable requests into bounded task plans and identifies required permissions up front.

nodes.label: Executor Role
nodes.rationale: Runs approved tools strictly one step at a time.

nodes.label: Observer Role
nodes.rationale: Collects UIA, DOM, application, screenshot, process and file state as the ground truth for verification.

nodes.label: Verifier Role
nodes.rationale: Determines whether each action and the final task actually succeeded — the enforcement point for honest task status.

nodes.label: Memory Curator Role
nodes.rationale: Proposes memory candidates and retrieves only relevant approved context into prompts.

nodes.label: Tool Contract
nodes.rationale: Every tool declares ID, version, description, input/output schema, risk category, permission requirements, resource locks, timeout, retry policy, state-changing flag, verification method, redaction rules, supported applications and failure codes — making permissions, locks and verification statically inspectable.

nodes.label: Structured Model Output Gate
nodes.rationale: Free-form natural language is never executed; every plan or tool call passes JSON/schema validation, permission evaluation, resource-lock evaluation, tool allow-list validation, parameter validation and user approval where required.

nodes.label: First-Run Onboarding Wizard
nodes.rationale: Detects hardware (CPU, RAM, GPU, VRAM, disk, Ollama, devices), recommends and downloads models only after approval with size and licence shown, configures wake phrase, voice, Brave profile, app discovery, startup, emergency-stop hotkey and permission policy, then runs a safe end-to-end test and offers .jarvispack import.

nodes.label: Signed Windows Installer and Updates
nodes.rationale: Per-user install, preserved data across updates, signed packages, rollback for failed updates, schema migrations and pack compatibility checks; large models are downloaded rather than bundled to keep the installer small and licensing clean.

nodes.label: Phased Delivery Plan (Phase 0-6)
nodes.rationale: Phase 0 safety architecture, 1 voice assistant, 2 deterministic automation, 3 tasks/macros/memory, 4 vision and long-running workflows, 5 IDE orchestration, 6 productisation. Building everything in one pass would yield an impressive demo and an unreliable product; a good first release does twenty approved tasks reliably instead of claiming it can do anything.

nodes.label: Project Jarvis Threat Model
nodes.rationale: Written against the full PRD surface (Phases 0-6) rather than only shipped Phase 0 code, so each phase can implement mitigations before shipping the capability that makes a threat reachable, instead of retrofitting safety after the fact.

nodes.label: STRIDE threat classification
nodes.rationale: Applied per trust-boundary crossing rather than per component, because threats materialise where data or control changes principal.

nodes.label: Prompt Injection (PI) category
nodes.rationale: Added because STRIDE alone does not capture a planner that consumes untrusted natural language and emits structured actions; untrusted content interpreted as instruction rather than data.

nodes.label: Tool Misuse (TM) category
nodes.rationale: The model selects, invents, or parameterises a tool in a way that is invalid, unscoped, or unsafe.

nodes.label: Over-Permission (OP) category
nodes.rationale: A capability grant is broader, longer-lived, or more reusable than the user's actual intent.

nodes.label: Hallucinated Success (HS) category
nodes.rationale: Jarvis reports or acts as though an outcome occurred without verifying it; honesty is treated as a security property, not a UX nicety.

nodes.label: Jarvis Core (orchestration, permissions, audit)
nodes.rationale: The trusted decision-making centre: tool registry, permission evaluation, planning, memory retrieval, and audit logging all concentrate here so a single choke point can be tested.

nodes.rationale: States per phase which mitigations must land before exit criteria are met, so a capability never ships ahead of the control that bounds it.

nodes.label: Residual risks accepted for Phase 0
nodes.rationale: A threat is 'live' only if the trust boundary and attacker capability it depends on already exist in code; the rest are modelled in advance and explicitly accepted as not reachable in Phase 0.

nodes.label: Security Policy and Control Specification
nodes.rationale: Deliberately separated from attacker modelling: this document is authoritative on control design, THREAT_MODEL.md is authoritative on the threat each control addresses.

nodes.label: Untrusted-data rule
nodes.rationale: All website content, documents, emails, messages, clipboard content and application text are data, never instructions; no text Jarvis reads, hears, transcribes or is shown may grant permission regardless of its claimed authority.

nodes.label: Closed authority set for tool authorisation
nodes.rationale: Only the authenticated local user, GUI settings, signed skill definitions, and system policy may authorise tools — an enumerated closed set rather than a trust heuristic.
nodes.norm_label: closed authority set for tool authorisation

nodes.label: Capability risk classification (low/medium/high/prohibited)
nodes.rationale: High-risk capabilities must not offer 'always allow', enforced as a structural constraint rather than a UI default a user could reconfigure around.

nodes.label: Prohibited capability class
nodes.rationale: Prohibited capabilities are compile-time absent, not runtime-denied: they must not be registered, must not appear in the tool schema exposed to the model, and must not be reachable by any code path.

nodes.label: Named prohibited broad tools
nodes.rationale: run_shell, execute_code, run_powershell, delete_anything, control_computer, approve_all, read_all_files and peers are banned by identifier and by equivalent effect regardless of name.

nodes.label: Static src/ scan for prohibited primitives
nodes.rationale: A build-time AST gate over subprocess, os.system, os.popen, eval(, exec(, shell=True and ShellExecute — catches a prohibited primitive before it ships rather than denying it at runtime.
nodes.norm_label: static src/ scan for prohibited primitives

nodes.label: Tool registry registration denylist
nodes.rationale: Second independent layer validating candidate tool ids and name patterns at registration, so a future contributor, plugin, or generated adapter cannot reintroduce a prohibited shape under a new name.

nodes.label: Permission model
nodes.rationale: Grants are revocable at any time including mid-task, which implies permission state must be re-checked at each tool invocation rather than cached for the task lifetime.

nodes.label: Permission decision types
nodes.rationale: Exhaustive closed set (Deny, Ask every time, session, task, application, folder, always for low-risk only); no new decision type without a PRD change.

nodes.label: Tool-invocation evaluation order
nodes.rationale: Prohibited and allow-list checks are sequenced ahead of schema and parameter validation as defence in depth — reject on identity before spending effort validating the shape of something that should never have been callable. Acknowledged as a known discrepancy with PRD §13.4's model-output chain, to be reconciled later.

nodes.label: Approval dialog required fields
nodes.rationale: A dialog that omits any applicable field (action, target, data, risk category, exact scope, reversibility) does not satisfy policy — the user cannot consent to what they cannot see.

nodes.label: Non-admin by default
nodes.rationale: The default state of the installed application, not a mode the user must remember to select.

nodes.label: Scoped elevation helper process
nodes.rationale: Per-action and process-isolated rather than in-process escalation: the helper performs one declared action and exits, never becoming a standing elevated service.

nodes.label: Secure desktop and UAC prompts off-limits
nodes.rationale: A deliberate limit that prevents Jarvis — or anything that has compromised Jarvis — from silently escalating privileges.
nodes.norm_label: secure desktop and uac prompts off-limits

nodes.label: Five-component process model
nodes.rationale: Audio and automation run outside the GUI thread even in the single-process MVP: a hang or crash there must not silently disable approvals, the audit log, or the permission engine in Core.

nodes.label: Local IPC requirements (loopback, per-install token)
nodes.rationale: Typed messages, loopback or named pipes only, per-installation token on every request, rejection of non-local interfaces, and token rotation on reset — a hard architectural requirement, not a loosenable default.

nodes.label: TTS worker isolation (Qwen3-TTS, separate env)
nodes.rationale: The template for any isolated worker: converts one narrow input into one narrow output and holds none of Core's authority — no direct access to Jarvis tools or permissions.

nodes.label: Secrets storage via DPAPI / Credential Manager
nodes.rationale: Never plaintext config, and no shared API keys shipped in the installer or source; passwords, payment data and password-manager content are a capture-time restriction, not an export-time redaction.
nodes.norm_label: secrets storage via dpapi / credential manager

nodes.label: .jarvispack normal-export secret exclusions
nodes.rationale: The default export path must never be able to leak secrets by omission of a filter; a separate passphrase-protected encrypted export is the sole path by which secrets may leave the local store.

nodes.label: Audit log requirements (append-only, redacted)
nodes.rationale: Redaction happens before the record is written, not as a display-time filter over a plaintext store; nothing lets a running process or the LLM edit prior entries, only explicit user-initiated deletion may remove history.

nodes.label: Screen capture scoping and screenshot retention
nodes.rationale: Capture is scoped to the minimum necessary surface (control, app, window, region, monitor) with full-desktop capture requiring explicit approval; screenshots are temporary by default and excluded from normal exports.
nodes.norm_label: screen capture scoping and screenshot retention

nodes.label: Telemetry off by default with content exclusions
nodes.norm_label: telemetry off by default with content exclusions

nodes.label: Root-scoped filesystem tools
nodes.rationale: There is no filesystem tool that operates against an unscoped or implicit 'whole computer' root; the unscoped shapes are on the prohibited list instead of being permission-gated.

nodes.label: Path canonicalisation before scope check
nodes.rationale: Relative paths, symlinks, junctions, shortcuts, case differences and environment variables are resolved before any scope check is considered satisfied; a path resolving outside the root is rejected, not merely flagged.

nodes.label: Absolutely denied filesystem targets
nodes.rationale: Credential stores, password databases, private keys, browser session databases and authentication files are denied independent of scope, so a legitimate folder grant can never become a credential-theft primitive.

nodes.label: Deletion is non-destructive by default
nodes.rationale: Recycle Bin plus explicit confirmation plus audit plus undo where possible; permanent deletion requires a separate high-risk confirmation stating the action cannot be undone.

nodes.label: Emergency stop surface
nodes.rationale: A cross-cutting control that must reach the Audio Worker, Automation Worker and Task Scheduler regardless of process boundary, and must release resource locks so a stopped task leaves nothing permanently held.

nodes.label: Dependency and licence scanning CI gate
nodes.rationale: Currently advisory (continue-on-error) via pip-audit and pip-licenses; becomes blocking before the first public build per ADR-0026.
nodes.norm_label: dependency and licence scanning ci gate

nodes.label: Phase 0 security status table
nodes.rationale: Verified against committed code and a passing suite (386 tests, 89% statement coverage), not the target design; every control not marked Implemented is a stated intention, not a working safeguard.

nodes.label: Tool invoker six-step pipeline (jarvis.core.tools.invoker)
nodes.rationale: Allow-list, schema, permission, locks, approval, execute as the single choke point, with bounded timeouts and retries and a 'succeeded' state that requires verification.

nodes.label: Approval port (deny by default)
nodes.rationale: With no approval dialog shipped yet, the Phase 0 default denies, so nothing requiring approval can run — an honest degraded state rather than an implicit allow.

nodes.label: Layering enforcement test (no Qt below presentation)
nodes.norm_label: layering enforcement test (no qt below presentation)

nodes.label: Ollama health check (loopback-only)
nodes.rationale: A non-loopback endpoint is refused without opening a socket; offline-mode aware and explicitly timed out.

nodes.label: Resource locks (jarvis.tasks.locks)
nodes.rationale: Exclusive, persisted, owner-attributed, acquired all-or-nothing over a sorted set to avoid deadlock, with stale reclamation after a crash.

nodes.label: ADR-0014: Default English Voice
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Records an already-made decision (Kokoro bm_george as default TTS) rather than opening a new one; the genuinely unresolved sub-question is narrower than 'which voice' - it is whether the voice pack and espeak-ng licences permit redistribution to third-party end users at Phase 6.

nodes.label: Kokoro bm_george Default Voice
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Chosen because it is CPU-only (zero VRAM cost, no contention with planner/vision models on the shared 12 GB RTX 5070 budget), has no runtime network dependency, and was already verified working end-to-end and encoded in config/defaults.yaml as text_to_speech.active_profile: kokoro_bm_george. Accepted over Piper (superseded in practice - reverting would discard tested configuration for no functional gain) and over SAPI-as-primary (noticeably lower quality, contradicts the local high-quality default product intent).

nodes.label: Windows SAPI Emergency Fallback
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Retained as fallback_only because it ships with Windows (zero download size, zero licensing risk), so the fallback path requires no extra download; promoting it to primary would be a regression from a verified working decision.

nodes.label: Voice Pack Redistribution Licensing Gap
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Kokoro-82M's weights carry a permissive licence favourable for redistribution, but the specific bm_george voice pack file and the bundled espeak-ng pronunciation dictionary (GPL-family) need licence terms re-verified at the exact pinned commit before an installer bundles or auto-downloads them. Hard deadline at Phase 6 because PRD §17.3 lists 'default voice with redistribution rights' as a precondition for public distribution.

nodes.label: espeak-ng GPL-Family Licensing Consideration
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: GPL obligations differ between 'installer downloads espeak-ng from its own installer at first run' and 'installer bundles espeak-ng binaries directly', so the licence check is coupled to the distribution model chosen in ADR-0013/ADR-0022.

nodes.label: Per-Download Provider and Licence Disclosure
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: PRD §17.2 requires every runtime download to show provider, licence, approximate size, install location, and redistribution status; this must be implemented in the first-run wizard regardless of the bundling answer, since even a first-run download needs this UI.

nodes.label: ADR-0015: Additional TTS Providers
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Accepted for the provider set, interface, and isolation model exactly as configured today; open only for the specific GPU scheduling-arbitration policy between strict exclusion and VRAM-budget co-residency.

nodes.label: Provider-Neutral TtsProvider Interface
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: FR-035 keeps provider-specific code out of conversation/task logic; ARCHITECTURE.md §8's extension-point table defines TtsProvider.speak(text, style) -> audio with exactly three consumers (Kokoro, SAPI fallback, Qwen3-TTS worker). Needed from Phase 1 even though the scheduler question is a Phase 4 concern.

nodes.label: Qwen3-TTS Isolated Python 3.12 Worker
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: FR-038 requires the Qwen3-TTS integration run as a separate process with typed authenticated local IPC, explicit health checks, bounded startup time, clean shutdown, and no direct access to Jarvis tools or permissions. Ships enabled: false, status experimental, so nothing blocks Phase 1-3 delivery.

nodes.label: Model Resource Scheduler (FR-039)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Prevents unsafe simultaneous loading of the planner model, vision model, GPU-backed TTS, and other high-memory GPU workloads via unloading, sequential loading, VRAM checks, provider fallback, and visible degradation status on the 12 GB RTX 5070 budget.

nodes.label: Option A: Strict Mutual Exclusion Scheduling
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: GPU-backed TTS treated as mutually exclusive with the vision model, matching the configured model_runtime.load_strategy: sequential and allow_parallel_heavy_models: false. Simplest to reason about and test, avoids VRAM exhaustion outright, but pays reload latency whenever vision and expressive speech are wanted close together.
nodes.norm_label: option a: strict mutual exclusion scheduling

nodes.label: Option B: VRAM-Budget-Aware Co-Residency
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Scheduler estimates each model's VRAM footprint and allows co-residency when the sum plus a safety margin fits in 12 GB. Better latency since Qwen3-TTS's 0.6B footprint is small relative to the 8-9B planner/vision models, but requires real VRAM measurement because KV-cache growth with context length matters, not just parameter-count arithmetic.

nodes.label: No Silent Voice Provider Switching (FR-036)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: A switch requires explicit user selection, a settings change, or a documented fallback caused by provider failure; any fallback must be displayed as temporary unavailability, not hidden. Accepted as a standing constraint (Option C) regardless of which arbitration policy governs the scheduler internals.

nodes.label: ADR-0016: Custom Jarvis Wake Word
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred to Phase 6. The gap between FR-011's stated 'Jarvis' default and the verified 'Hey Jarvis' model is treated as an honest gap to name rather than silently resolve, per PRD §4.6's honest-task-status principle.

nodes.label: Hey Jarvis Interim Wake Phrase
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: openWakeWord ships pretrained models for common phrases including 'Hey Jarvis', so this is the verified working default configured today, with desired_phrase: Jarvis recorded separately as the unmet product target. The GUI must not claim 'Jarvis' alone is detected until a custom model is actually trained and measured, per FR-011's explicit prohibition.

nodes.label: Option A: Purpose-Trained Custom Jarvis Wake Model
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: A bare single-word wake phrase is materially harder to train reliably because shorter phrases have fewer distinguishing phonetic features, raising false-activation rate unless trained with curated multi-speaker positives and hard negatives against acoustically similar words. Cost includes data collection, training compute, credible false-activation evaluation, and its own distribution/licensing answer since it is not a pretrained artefact.
nodes.norm_label: option a: purpose-trained custom jarvis wake model

nodes.label: False-Activation Evaluation Harness
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: A custom model must achieve a false-activation rate at or below the measured rate of the pretrained 'Hey Jarvis' model - it must not merely work sometimes, it must not regress reliability. A wake model that mis-fires disrupts an always-listening assistant more than a slightly longer phrase costs. The harness cost (test audio corpus, methodology) must be scoped before committing.

nodes.label: Push-to-Talk Global Hotkey Fallback
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: FR-018's configurable global-hotkey push-to-talk sidesteps false-activation risk and must remain available and discoverable regardless of which wake-phrase option is chosen, since FR-011 requires it as a fallback when wake detection is unreliable. Making it the primary default (Option C) would undercut the voice-first product framing of the §8.1 persona.

nodes.label: ADR-0017: Embedding Model
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Proposed, not Accepted: qwen3-embedding:0.6b is a working default, not a benchmarked one - unlike the TTS voice or screenshot retention defaults, PROJECT_INPUTS.md carries no verified marker for it.

nodes.label: qwen3-embedding:0.6b Tentative Default
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Kept as the working development default so Phase 3 memory-retrieval work is not blocked. Pros: already wired into the Ollama routing path, same model family as planner/vision (simplifying tokenizer/quantization tooling and reducing distinct families to test), small enough to plausibly stay resident alongside the planner. Cons: no recorded dimensionality, benchmark latency, or retrieval-quality measurement exists.

nodes.label: Rebuildable Derived Index Constraint
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: ARCHITECTURE.md §9 and PRD §14.1 require the embedding index, file index, and caches be derived and rebuildable, never holding unique information. This lowers the stakes of the model choice considerably: switching models later means recomputing the index, not migrating or losing data - so the question is reindex time, not feasibility.

nodes.label: Embedding Invocation Frequency Cost
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: The embedding model is the most frequently invoked of the three roles - plausibly every memory write and retrieval touches it, unlike the planner (per-turn) or vision (occasional) - so latency and co-residency behaviour with the planner matter more than raw parameter size alone would suggest.

nodes.label: Option B: Dedicated Retrieval-Purpose-Built Embedding Model
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: A BGE- or Nomic-family model is purpose-built for embeddings rather than being a chat-model family's embedding head, and often has well-published independently reproduced retrieval benchmarks that de-risk FR-163 retrieval quality. Cost: a different model family means a separate download, separate licence check, and one more entry in the model-compatibility test matrix.
nodes.norm_label: option b: dedicated retrieval-purpose-built embedding model

nodes.label: Option C: First-Run Wizard Hardware Benchmark
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Most honest given the tentative status - defers the choice to measured reality on the actual target machine rather than a documentation-time guess, extending the existing hardware-assessment framework. But risks blocking Phase 3 memory work on wizard engineering that is more naturally a Phase 6 concern.
nodes.norm_label: option c: first-run wizard hardware benchmark

nodes.label: ADR-0018: Search Provider
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred. The open question is scope, not mechanism: visible Brave search is mandatory and needs no external account, so what remains open is whether Jarvis also offers a programmatic search path and with what built-in provider integration.

nodes.label: Visible Brave Search Mode (FR-052)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Performing the search visibly rather than headlessly is a deliberate transparency choice, not an implementation detail - a hard product requirement not contingent on this ADR. It is the safe Phase 2 floor: zero-key, satisfies the Definition of Done item 'search the internet, show sources' without any external account setup.

nodes.label: Option B: Optional User-Supplied Search API Key
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Completes FR-050's mode set with faster in-conversation answers; the key is explicitly user-owned so §18.3 is satisfied by construction as long as storage goes through the Windows-protected credential store rather than user.yaml. Cost: the product needs an opinion on which APIs it supports, and a programmatic path is a different untrusted-content channel, not an inherently safer one.
nodes.norm_label: option b: optional user-supplied search api key

nodes.label: No Shared API Keys Constraint (§18.3)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Any search-provider key, cloud-model key, TTS key, or integration token must be user-supplied and stored in Windows-protected credential storage, not plaintext configuration. Verifiable by inspection: a test can assert no default or example API key exists anywhere in config/defaults.yaml or the codebase. Under Option A this becomes structurally impossible to violate because no key-consuming code path exists.

nodes.label: Untrusted Web Content Wrapping (FR-054)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Instructions found on web pages are never treated as agent instructions or tool-call authority - ARCHITECTURE.md §7's principle that untrusted content 'can inform a plan; it can never authorise a capability', enforced by §11.4's delimiter-wrapping strategy. Must be implemented for every enabled mode, since an API-search result is exactly as untrusted as a scraped web page.

nodes.label: Option C: Ask a Configured AI Website (FR-055)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Opens a configured AI website in the dedicated profile, enters the user's prompt, and optionally reads back the answer. Largest scope - FR-055 has its own substantial requirements (must not scrape unrelated conversation history, waits for completion, notifies) that are really a Phase 2/5 browser-automation deliverable, so bundling it here risks conflating 'which search modes exist' with 'how well is each one built'.
nodes.norm_label: option c: ask a configured ai website (fr-055)

nodes.label: ADR-0019: Browser Profile Isolation
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred, but Option C is effectively ruled out by the existing commitment to Brave, narrowing the real choice to isolation strength (separate user-data-dir) versus native-profile fidelity (Brave profile directory).

nodes.label: Dedicated Jarvis Brave Profile
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: The name and existence are already fixed by PROJECT_INPUTS.md (automation.dedicated_browser_profile: Jarvis); what is unfixed is the mechanism. This matters more than an ordinary implementation detail because once a user logs into email, shopping, or work services inside it, live authenticated sessions are under the product's control - any defect, successful prompt injection, or overly broad tool scope can act as the logged-in user.

nodes.label: Option A: Brave --profile-directory Mechanism
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Closest to 'the user's actual Brave' - extensions and browser chrome behave exactly as a manually opened profile, which matters for the CAPTCHA-pause requirement since a genuinely normal window is what the user interacts with. Cons: shares the underlying Brave installation surface with the user's default profile, and Playwright's CDP attachment to a named profile (rather than a fresh data directory) needs verification.

nodes.label: Option B: Separate --user-data-dir Under the Vault
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Strongest filesystem-level separation - a defect that reads or writes browser-profile files cannot reach the user's personal Brave data at all. Matches the documented vault layout (ProjectJarvis\browser\brave-profile\), so relocatability and full deletability fall out of the existing vault design for free, and FR-057's 'clear the profile' becomes 'delete this directory'. Cost: first-run interstitials the automation must dismiss, and no inherited extensions.
nodes.norm_label: option b: separate --user-data-dir under the vault

nodes.label: Option C: Playwright Bundled Chromium Persistent Context
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Best-documented and most reliable Playwright automation surface with the fewest CDP-attachment surprises, but directly contradicts §12.1's explicit 'Dedicated persistent Brave profile' commitment - plausibly made for Brave's ad/tracker-blocking defaults, which matter for a browser the agent controls. Substituting bundled Chromium would be a PRD deviation requiring its own justification.
nodes.norm_label: option c: playwright bundled chromium persistent context

nodes.label: CAPTCHA Pause-and-Ask Requirement (FR-058)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Jarvis pauses and asks the user to complete CAPTCHAs or anti-bot challenges rather than attempt to bypass them - §11.1 lists CAPTCHA bypass as a prohibited capability. The pause must hand control to the user in a window they can interact with normally, with no automation-imposed friction such as remote-debugging banners making the CAPTCHA harder than in an ordinary browser.

nodes.label: ADR-0020: Plugin and Skill Signing
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred. Given single-developer, local-first scope with no stated marketplace, no-signing is the pragmatic near-term floor with self-signed keys as the natural next step if packs start moving between people who are not the developer.

nodes.label: Skill Manifest signed Field
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: §14.5's schema already includes signed: false as a first-class always-present element. That the field exists and defaults to false while no signing mechanism exists is itself informative - the schema was designed anticipating this ADR's outcome without presupposing it. It must remain a visible, honest field: a signed: false pack must never be displayed ambiguously alongside a signed: true one.

nodes.label: .jarvispack Imported Skill Pack
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: The specific attack surface this ADR addresses. A skill is not inert data: it declares required_permissions, required_apps, and resource_locks, and its workflow.json entrypoint encodes UI Automation elements, browser selectors, and keyboard/mouse actions that execute through the same ToolInvoker pipeline as any other agent-proposed action. created_by already tracks imported provenance as a distinct category.

nodes.label: Option A: Approval-Only Gate, No Signing
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Relies entirely on FR-105's explicit approval before any skill activates plus the permission engine's per-capability evaluation. Zero infrastructure cost, and keeps signed: false simply true for everything, which is honest rather than a half-built feature. But it does nothing to help a user judge before approval whether a pack is unmodified or really from the claimed author, relying on the user reading a possibly-long permission list correctly every time - exactly the approval-fatigue risk signing schemes exist to mitigate.
nodes.norm_label: option a: approval-only gate, no signing

nodes.label: Option B: Self-Signed Developer Keys
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Authors generate their own key; Jarvis verifies signatures and displays a stable author fingerprint so a user can tell 'this is the same author as last time' and detect in-transit tampering, without any central registry. Cheap and consistent with the local-first, no-central-dependency posture, but proves internal consistency, not trustworthiness - a naive 'Signed' badge would overstate the guarantee.

nodes.label: Option C: Project-Operated Signing Authority
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Strongest guarantee and closest to what users assume 'signed' means, but carries substantial ongoing operational cost disproportionate for a single-owner local-first project with no stated marketplace, and introduces a dependency on project-owner availability contradicting the no-required-backend philosophy elsewhere in the PRD.

nodes.label: ADR-0021: Encrypted Sync and Backup
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred. Local backup only is the safe, low-cost default consistent with §4.1, the telemetry-off default, and the no-shared-secrets posture, and is likely sufficient unless real demand for cross-machine continuity emerges.

nodes.label: Option A: Local Backup Only, No Network Transport
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Zero new secret-handling surface since nothing is ever transmitted, no dependency on a third party's availability or pricing, and the simplest possible position to defend in a security review. Cost: cross-machine continuity is entirely the user's manual responsibility and there is no protection against local drive failure.
nodes.norm_label: option a: local backup only, no network transport

nodes.label: Option B: User-Supplied Cloud Storage with Client-Side Encryption
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: The user points Jarvis at storage they already control, encrypted client-side so the third party only sees ciphertext, keeping the product free of any backend to operate. Cost: key derivation/management, conflict handling across two machines, versioning so a schema migration on one machine does not produce an unreadable backup on another, plus new steady-state failure modes like partial upload and permanent encryption-key loss.
nodes.norm_label: option b: user-supplied cloud storage with client-side encryption

nodes.label: Off-Device Backup Compromise Surface
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Sync that leaves the device is qualitatively different from local export because it turns a single compromise point (this machine) into two (this machine and wherever the backup lives), and because cloud storage implies an ongoing third-party relationship the product does not otherwise require.

nodes.label: Portable Identity Export (FR-168)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Covers personality, preferences, memories, application aliases, skills, permissions template, model selections, voice selections, task templates, prompt templates, and optionally conversation history. Already a Phase 3 baseline, which is why deferring sync costs mostly opportunity rather than blocking anything.

nodes.label: Secret Exclusion from Normal Exports (FR-169/FR-170)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: API keys, cookies, tokens, and credentials are excluded from normal exports; secrets may only travel via a separate, optional, explicitly warned, passphrase-protected encrypted export. Must be verifiably enforced by test for any backup or sync path chosen, and the passphrase should ideally never leave the local Windows-protected credential store.

nodes.label: ADR-0022: MSIX Distribution
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred, leaning to classic-installer-primary. The real question is not 'MSIX or not at all' but 'MSIX-as-primary versus MSIX-as-optional-secondary'. Must close before ADR-0013 is finalised to avoid circular blocking, since whether MSIX is primary materially changes what the installer ADR needs to decide.

nodes.label: MSIX Sandboxing vs Desktop Automation Tension
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: MSIX's filesystem/registry virtualization and AppContainer-style sandbox are in real tension with what the product structurally needs: the scoped-elevation helper, UI Automation driving arbitrary third-party windows, global hotkeys and emergency stop, startup registration, and a user-relocatable vault outside the package's storage area. Some are outright restricted under full Store sandboxing; others require sparse-package hybrids or review-gated capability declarations.
nodes.norm_label: msix sandboxing vs desktop automation tension

nodes.label: Option A: MSIX as Primary Distribution Format
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Clean uninstall via virtualization, built-in update infrastructure if Store-distributed, and per-user install as MSIX's default posture. But Store certification would review an app whose entire purpose is automating other applications and reading screen content - a category that historically draws extra scrutiny - and the unpackaged-plus-MSIX-installer hybrid workaround somewhat defeats the sandboxing benefit that motivated choosing MSIX.
nodes.norm_label: option a: msix as primary distribution format

nodes.label: Option B: MSIX as Secondary Optional Channel
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: The lower-risk starting lean: the primary distribution path stays unconstrained by sandboxing limits so elevation, UI Automation, global hotkeys, and vault relocation all work as designed, while MSIX remains a genuine convenience without gating the product's architecture on satisfying its constraints. Cost: two packaging pipelines for a small project, and a possibly feature-limited MSIX variant risking user confusion.
nodes.norm_label: option b: msix as secondary optional channel

nodes.label: ADR-0023: Adapter Isolation
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred; in-process is the correct posture through Phase 0-1 since no adapters exist yet to isolate, but the decision must close before Phase 2. Deferral cost rises sharply at the Phase 2 boundary because every additional in-process adapter is one more component needing retrofit into a process boundary later. Note: ARCHITECTURE.md cross-references this decision under two stale placeholder numbers (ADR-0004 and ADR-0010); reconciliation is out of scope here.

nodes.label: AppAdapter Extension Point
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: ARCHITECTURE.md §8 defines the interface (launch, verify, close, actions) with Brave, YouTube, Xbox, and Antigravity as first consumers across Phases 2 and 5. Whether it stabilises before Phase 2 is itself a decision criterion, since IPC/serialization cost should not fight a still-changing contract.

nodes.label: In-Process Isolation Is Not a Security Boundary
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: ARCHITECTURE.md §13 gap 2: in Phases 0-3 a defect in the automation worker can reach the vault. Prompt-injection defence wraps untrusted content at the planning-and-tool-call layer, but does not protect against a defect in an adapter itself - a parsing error or unvalidated selector - being triggered by crafted content. In-process, such a defect runs with the same privileges as jarvis.core and jarvis.storage, which share the vault's process.
nodes.norm_label: in-process isolation is not a security boundary

nodes.label: Option A: In-Process Adapters (Status Quo)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Zero migration cost, matches ARCHITECTURE.md §4.1's deliberate single-process design for Phases 0-3, avoids IPC/serialization/authentication overhead, and keeps velocity high while the AppAdapter interface is still iterating. Cons: the named security gap persists, a crash in one adapter can destabilise the whole process, and adapter dependency conflicts have no isolation to fall back on.

nodes.label: Option B: Isolated Plugin Process Per Adapter
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: The security boundary becomes real: a compromised or crashing adapter cannot directly read jarvis.db, in-process secret material, or other adapters' state. Not a novel pattern - it reuses the typed authenticated local IPC already accepted for the Qwen3-TTS worker and anticipated for the elevated-action helper. Cost: every call becomes cross-process with schema validation, timeouts and authentication; the permission engine and audit log must attribute actions back to the originating task; more processes means memory/startup overhead.
nodes.norm_label: option b: isolated plugin process per adapter

nodes.label: Option C: Isolate Only Highest-Risk Adapters
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Keeps low-risk adapters in-process while isolating those touching high-risk surfaces - browser automation in a logged-in profile, and IDE adapters that must never auto-approve terminal commands or credential access. Concentrates isolation cost where the security argument is strongest, but requires a maintained risk classification that can drift as adapters gain capabilities, and two execution models may be more total complexity than one consistent model.
nodes.norm_label: option c: isolate only highest-risk adapters

nodes.label: Automation Worker Adversarial Input Exposure
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Adapters and the Automation Worker are the components most exposed to untrusted adversarial input - screen content, DOM content, and UI Automation trees are all partially controlled by a third-party application or a malicious website rendered inside the dedicated Brave profile.

nodes.label: ADR-0024: Data Retention Defaults
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred with per-stream defaults as the leading candidate. Must close before the first Phase 3 write path lands, because retrofitting expiry to data collected under 'keep forever' means either deleting data the user was implicitly promised, or grandfathering it and living with two regimes.

nodes.label: Option B: Per-Stream Retention Defaults with Expiry
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Proportionate: sensitive low-value streams (clipboard 24h off-by-default, notification events 30 days) expire quickly while safety-relevant streams (audit log 365 days, never off) are kept, bounding growth without silently losing high-value data. Proposed defaults include conversation history 90 days, memory candidates 14 days, task records 90 days after terminal state, approved memories no expiry. Cost: an expiry sweep is a new background job that must never run mid-task, and users must understand different screens forget at different rates.
nodes.norm_label: option b: per-stream retention defaults with expiry

nodes.label: Option A: Keep Everything Until User Deletes
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Simplest to implement and explain, never loses something the user wanted, maximum retrieval quality, and matches how Phase 0 already behaves. But unbounded growth makes the vault the single richest target on the machine, 'I deleted that months ago' turns out to be false, and the entire hygiene burden falls on the user.
nodes.norm_label: option a: keep everything until user deletes

nodes.label: Option C: One Global Retention Period
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: One control the user actually understands, but wrong for every stream simultaneously - either the clipboard is kept far too long or the audit log is destroyed while it is still the only evidence of what the agent did. Conflates a safety record with a convenience cache.
nodes.norm_label: option c: one global retention period

nodes.label: Cascade Deletion of Derived Data (FR-167)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deleting source material must offer to delete what was derived from it - a retention policy that expires a conversation but leaves its embeddings behind is not deletion. Cascade-on-expiry needs the same care as cascade-on-delete, and rebuildable derived indexes are what make cascade deletion safe.

nodes.label: Audit Log as a Safety Record
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: The audit log pulls against the exposure-minimisation argument: it is a safety record, and aggressively expiring it would remove the user's ability to review what the agent did. Its default must never be zero and it cannot be disabled entirely; the retention sweep itself must also be audited so the user can see that data was removed and how much.
nodes.norm_label: audit log as a safety record

nodes.label: Clipboard History Retention (FR-253)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Proposed 24 hours and off by default because it carries the highest sensitivity per byte of any retained stream.

nodes.label: ADR-0025: Maximum Screenshot Retention
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Accepted for the task_only default as already configured; the diagnostic ceiling, the failed-task extension window, and the selected-mode confirmation model remain open until Phase 4. The cost concentrates at one point: the first Phase 4 capture must already know its retention rule, because a screenshot written under an undecided policy is a screenshot with no deletion schedule.

nodes.label: task_only Screenshot Retention Default
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Screenshots live only as long as the task that produced them and are deleted at terminal state, giving the smallest exposure window with no accumulation. Chosen because screen captures are the highest-risk artefact the product will ever write to disk - a single screenshot can contain an authentication code, a bank balance, a private message, or a password manager mid-reveal, sometimes belonging to somebody else.

nodes.label: Option B: Extended Retention for Failed Tasks
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Screenshots attached to a failed or blocked task survive a bounded period (proposed 7 days) so the user can inspect the failure, aligning retention with the honesty requirement - a task claiming failure should be able to show why. But failure is correlated with unusual screen states, exactly when a screenshot is most likely to have caught something unexpected, so the extended window carries disproportionate risk and needs sensitive-application exclusions applied at retention time, not just capture time.
nodes.norm_label: option b: extended retention for failed tasks

nodes.label: Option C: Diagnostic Mode with Global Disk Budget
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Diagnostic mode keeps everything up to a byte ceiling (proposed 500 MB and 14 days, whichever binds first), evicting oldest-first. Bounds disk regardless of behaviour, but oldest-first eviction is not risk-aware - it can retain a sensitive capture while discarding a harmless one. A disk budget is not a privacy control, and presenting it as one would be misleading.
nodes.norm_label: option c: diagnostic mode with global disk budget

nodes.label: Blocked-Capture Application Exclusions (FR-273)
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Users may block capture entirely for named applications and Jarvis must refuse rather than capture them. The exclusion is enforced at capture time, not at display time, so a screenshot from a blocked application is never written to disk at all. Complemented by narrowest-sufficient-target scoping (control, then window, then region, then monitor), a visible capture indicator, and exclusion from normal exports.

nodes.label: Expired Screenshot Evidence Must Degrade Honestly
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: A screenshot referenced as task evidence is either retained as long as the evidence claim stands, or the evidence record states that the image has expired - never a dangling path presented as if it were viewable. Verification evidence is what makes the honesty requirement enforceable rather than aspirational.
nodes.norm_label: expired screenshot evidence must degrade honestly

nodes.label: ADR-0026: Code-Signing and Update Infrastructure
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Deferred, with OV-certificate plus manual updates as the leading candidate and a documented migration path to EV plus automatic checks once there is a user base worth updating automatically. Provenance is a functional requirement, not a formality: an unsigned agent asking to automate a desktop is exactly what a cautious user should refuse.

nodes.label: Option A: OV Certificate with Manual Update Checks
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: Lowest cost and least infrastructure, and a manual-only check means the update path cannot be triggered remotely, removing a whole class of attack. But SmartScreen reputation must be earned so early users still see a warning - for a desktop automation agent, precisely the audience most likely to abandon the install - and security fixes propagate only as fast as users check manually, so a serious fix needs an out-of-band announcement channel.
nodes.norm_label: option a: ov certificate with manual update checks

nodes.label: Option B: EV Certificate with Optional Automatic Checks
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: An EV certificate on a hardware token or cloud HSM grants immediate SmartScreen reputation with no warning from the first install, and security fixes actually reach users. Materially more expensive, requires HSM-based signing in CI, and the automatic update path must be secured properly with signature verification before execution, rollback on failure, and no silent downgrade.
nodes.norm_label: option b: ev certificate with optional automatic checks

nodes.label: SmartScreen Reputation Barrier
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: An unsigned installer triggers an 'unrecognised app' warning most users read as 'this is malware'. An OV certificate removes the unknown-publisher wording but not the reputation warning, which clears only after enough installs accumulate; an EV certificate grants reputation immediately but requires a hardware token or cloud HSM at several times the cost.

nodes.label: Signature Verification Precedes Execution
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: An update package whose signature does not verify is discarded, not warned about - testable with a deliberately corrupted package. An update mechanism that can install code is by construction the highest-value target in the product: compromising it compromises every installation at once.

nodes.label: Update Rollback and Schema Compatibility Checks
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: A failed update must restore the previous version and its data intact, including a half-applied schema migration. Schema compatibility is checked before an update installs, not after, because a database newer than the incoming binary is already a hard startup failure the updater must not create. Incompatible skills are disabled with an explanation rather than silently failing at run time, downgrade is never silent, and the user can decline updates entirely.
nodes.norm_label: update rollback and schema compatibility checks

nodes.label: Update Package Format and Manifest Schema
nodes.author: Project owner
nodes.rationale: The one thing that should not wait for Phase 6: retrofitting a signature envelope onto an already-shipped format means supporting two formats forever. The artefact format and manifest schema are designed so that adding automatic checks later does not change the update package format, keeping the expensive infrastructure deferred without painting the project into a corner. Separately, the first artefact handed to anyone outside the project must be signed - an unsigned build in circulation, even briefly, establishes exactly the habit this decision exists to prevent.
nodes.norm_label: update package format and manifest schema

nodes.label: Arc Reactor Visual Motif
nodes.rationale: The mark reproduces the Iron Man arc reactor silhouette (circular metallic chassis, three outer arc segments, inverted triangular glowing core). Chosen because the product is named Jarvis after the Iron Man AI assistant, so the reactor reads as an instantly recognizable shorthand for 'personal AI assistant' without needing any text in the icon.

nodes.label: Circular Metallic Chassis Ring
nodes.rationale: A brushed grey/silver bevelled ring frames the whole mark and bleeds to the edge of the square canvas. A full-bleed circular silhouette survives the aggressive circular and rounded-square masking applied by Windows taskbar, Start menu, and MSIX tile rendering, so no content is lost at small sizes.

nodes.label: Inverted Triangular Glowing Core
nodes.rationale: Nested downward-pointing triangles with a white blown-out center form the focal point. The strong single geometric shape stays legible when the icon is downsampled to 16x16 or 32x32, where the finer arc segments collapse into an undifferentiated ring.

nodes.label: Cyan-on-White Emissive Palette
nodes.rationale: Saturated cyan strokes over near-white fills simulate an emissive light source through pure flat vector shapes rather than raster blur, so the asset rescales cleanly. High-luminance cyan also holds contrast against both light and dark Windows themes.

nodes.label: Transparent Alpha Square Canvas
nodes.rationale: The PNG keeps a transparent square background outside the circular disc so the icon composites over arbitrary shell backgrounds and can be converted to .ico / MSIX asset sizes without re-cutting a matte.

nodes.label: Jarvis Product Brand Identity
nodes.rationale: The icon is the only visual brand artifact in resources/icons and carries the entire product identity for shell surfaces (window icon, tray icon, installer, shortcut). Its borrowed Iron Man arc reactor imagery ties the internal codename 'Jarvis' to a visual, which is a trademark exposure the public-facing product name decision has to reconcile.

nodes.label: Architectural Drivers
nodes.rationale: Five prioritised requirements shape every structural decision; where they conflict the higher-numbered driver loses. A sixth softer driver is that the architecture must survive replacing the Python shell with a native shell (ADR-0001), which is why every cross-component message is a typed model and JarvisCore never imports Qt.

nodes.label: Closed Capability Set (no generic execution primitive)
nodes.rationale: The agent must never obtain unrestricted computer control (PRD 6.1, 11.1, 13.3), so capabilities are a closed enumerated set and no generic execution primitive can be added without failing a build test.
nodes.norm_label: closed capability set (no generic execution primitive)

nodes.label: Single Choke Point for Tool Execution
nodes.rationale: Every consequential action must be auditable, interruptible and attributable, which is only achievable if one component mediates all execution and nothing bypasses it; every action therefore carries a task ID.
nodes.norm_label: single choke point for tool execution

nodes.label: Model Output Is Untrusted Input
nodes.rationale: The LLM emits structured tool-call proposals which are validated, permission-checked and lock-checked before execution. Free text is never executed.

nodes.label: Single-Process Multi-Thread Model
nodes.rationale: Phases 0-3 run shell, core, scheduler and workers in one Windows process. Separation is enforced by module boundaries and typed messages rather than process isolation, so promoting a component to its own process later requires no interface change.

nodes.label: Qt Main Thread Must Not Block
nodes.rationale: Audio, inference, automation and I/O run on worker threads so the UI stays responsive (PRD NFR-003). The Qt main thread only paints and dispatches.
nodes.norm_label: qt main thread must not block

nodes.label: Deferred Process Separation (TTS worker, elevation helper)
nodes.rationale: The Qwen3-TTS worker needs Python 3.12 and CUDA, a dependency set that conflicts with the host; the elevated action helper needs UAC. Both will use named pipes or loopback only, with a per-installation authentication token and rotation on reset.
nodes.norm_label: deferred process separation (tts worker, elevation helper)

nodes.label: Concurrency Invariants
nodes.rationale: Tasks run concurrently only with disjoint lock sets; at most one holds foreground_desktop; lock acquisition is all-or-nothing in canonical sorted order to prevent deadlock; locks record an owning runtime instance so stale ones are reclaimed at startup; pause is cooperative and lands at a declared checkpoint, never mid-action.

nodes.label: Six-Layer Dependency Model (L0-L5)
nodes.rationale: Dependencies point downward only: common, then storage/config/diagnostics, then core, then capability modules, then runtime, then ui. A test enforces it so the engine stays importable and testable headlessly and the GUI is a replaceable adapter.

nodes.label: Only L5 May Import PySide6
nodes.rationale: jarvis.core, jarvis.tasks, jarvis.storage, jarvis.llm and jarvis.config must not import PySide6. jarvis.main imports Qt lazily inside a function so --check runs with no display and no Qt loaded at all.

nodes.label: Tool Machinery in L2, Tool Implementations in L3
nodes.rationale: jarvis.core.tools holds the contract, registry and invoker; jarvis.toolbox holds the tools, because an implementation may need a capability module that L2 must not import. The invoker depends on the lock manager only through a protocol in jarvis.core.tools.ports, never on jarvis.tasks directly.
nodes.norm_label: tool machinery in l2, tool implementations in l3

nodes.label: Layered Configuration System (jarvis.config)
nodes.rationale: Three layers merged deepest-first (shipped defaults, user overrides, JARVIS_* environment variables) then validated into one frozen pydantic AppConfig with extra=forbid and a pinned schema_version.

nodes.label: Override-Only Persistence
nodes.rationale: user.yaml stores only the difference from defaults, so upgrading defaults changes behaviour for untouched settings and never silently reverts a user's choice. Writes are atomic (temp file in the same directory, then rename) so a crash mid-save cannot corrupt configuration.

nodes.label: extra=forbid Everywhere
nodes.rationale: A typo in a settings key becomes a startup error naming the exact path rather than a silently ignored value.

nodes.label: VaultPaths (centralised path resolution)
nodes.rationale: jarvis.config.paths.VaultPaths is the only code that expands %LOCALAPPDATA% and %USERPROFILE%. JARVIS_DATA_DIR relocates the entire vault, which is how every test gets an isolated vault and how PRD 14.2 relocation is implemented.

nodes.label: Typed In-Process Event Bus (jarvis.core.events)
nodes.rationale: Frozen pydantic events with subclass matching; publishing is thread-safe and a raising handler is logged and isolated so it never breaks the publisher or other subscribers. Deliberately not a message broker: it does not persist, retry or order across threads, and anything needing durability goes through the task store.

nodes.label: EventBridge (domain events to queued Qt signals)
nodes.rationale: The GUI never subscribes to the bus directly. jarvis.ui.qt_bridge.EventBridge subscribes once and re-emits as queued Qt signals; it is the only place where the domain and Qt threading models meet.
nodes.norm_label: eventbridge (domain events to queued qt signals)

nodes.label: Dual-Sink Append-Only Audit Log (jarvis.core.audit)
nodes.rationale: logs/audit.jsonl is the tamper-evident record (fsync on write); the SQLite audit_event table is a rebuildable query index. Fields follow PRD 11.5 exactly.

nodes.label: Redaction Before Serialisation
nodes.rationale: redaction.py walks the parameter tree and replaces values whose key matches a secret pattern (password, token, api_key, secret, cookie, authorization, passphrase, private_key, credential, otp) and values that look like secrets (PEM blocks, bearer tokens, long high-entropy hex). Clipboard content is never logged in plaintext, only a length and a content class. Oversized strings are truncated with an explicit marker so a log entry cannot smuggle out a document.

nodes.label: Permission Engine (jarvis.core.permissions)
nodes.rationale: Answers one question - may this capability run, in this scope, right now - and never executes anything. Evaluation short-circuits: unknown capability denies, PROHIBITED denies unconditionally and cannot be configured away, HIGH always asks, then matching grant, then configured default policy.
